# **Automotive Cabin Acoustics and Automated Defect Detection via Single-Point MEMS Measurement**

## **Theoretical Foundations of Automotive In-Cabin Acoustics**

The acoustic characterization of an automotive passenger compartment using a single, fixed, uncalibrated Micro-Electromechanical Systems (MEMS) microphone presents a highly constrained signal processing challenge. Automotive cabins are irregular, highly damped, asymmetric acoustic cavities characterized by complex boundary conditions and low-frequency vibro-acoustic coupling. Unlike standard architectural acoustics, the interior space of a motor vehicle transitions radically between distinct physical regimes depending on the frequency of the excitation signal.  
At high frequencies, sound propagation behaves as a stochastic ray-tracing phenomenon, dominated by specular reflections off hard boundaries such as the windshield, side glass, and dashboard. In the midrange, wave interference creates complex comb-filtering patterns and spatial nulls, heavily influenced by the physical dimensions of the occupants and seating materials. At low frequencies, typically below ![][image1], the acoustic environment transitions into a modal regime where standing waves dictate the sound pressure level at any given point in the space1. Finally, at the lowest frequencies, the wavelength of the sound exceeds the longest dimension of the cabin, causing the space to cease functioning as a resonant wave-guide and instead operate as a pneumatic pressure vessel, a phenomenon commonly referred to as cabin gain3.  
The physical parameters of the vehicle are defined by standardized measurement protocols, most notably SAE J1100, which establishes the Seating Reference Point (SgRP) and defines the geometric boundaries of the occupant compartment5. However, these standardized dimensions do not always correlate directly to the acoustic volume perceived by a sound wave. For instance, low-frequency acoustic waves easily penetrate the rear seat structures of standard sedans, meaning the effective acoustic length of the cavity extends well into the trunk space7.

## **Signal Processing Constraints and Hardware Limitations**

The system relies on an Android head unit utilizing the Unisoc UIS7862 (QF/K706 platform) processor to capture and analyze the acoustic environment. The primary sensor is a built-in, uncalibrated MEMS microphone, typically recessed behind a ![][image2] to ![][image3] pinhole in the fascia2. This physical housing fundamentally alters the microphone's frequency response, creating a Helmholtz resonator effect that introduces unpredictable peaks in the upper midrange and acts as a steep low-pass filter at the highest audible frequencies. Because the microphone is uncalibrated, absolute Sound Pressure Level (SPL) measurements are impossible; all analysis must rely on relative magnitude differences across a ![][image4]\-band fractional-octave spectrum and the temporal data derived from the impulse response.  
The acoustic measurement is performed by playing an exponential sine sweep (Logarithmic Sweep Sine) from ![][image5] to ![][image6] (or from ![][image7] for the subwoofer channel) and recording the room response at a sample rate of ![][image8]1. The recorded signal is then deconvolved against the inverse of the excitation signal to extract the system's impulse response10. From this impulse response, the system utilizes the Generalized Cross-Correlation with Phase Transform (GCC-PHAT) algorithm to calculate the Time of Arrival (ToA) for each speaker channel3. By comparing the ToA across channels, the algorithm can calculate the exact acoustic delay required to time-align the direct sound arrivals at the microphone position.  
The equalization hardware is heavily constrained. The ROHM BU32107 chip, managed via a microcontroller, provides only coarse, global correction. It features a single ![][image4]\-band Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) equalizer applied to all channels simultaneously, placed before the subwoofer crossover. The Quality factor (Q) of these filters is fixed at ![][image9], and adjustments can only be made in ![][image10] steps up to a maximum of ![][image11]3. A Q factor of ![][image9] corresponds to a bandwidth of approximately ![][image12] octaves, meaning the equalizer is fundamentally incapable of addressing narrow, high-Q modal peaks or sharp reflection nulls. Because independent per-channel equalization is impossible with this hardware topology, the system cannot correct for the inevitable left-right path length asymmetries or localized speaker resonances1. Consequently, the system's primary utility shifts from achieving a perfectly flat target curve to performing automated acoustic defect detection and providing rudimentary global tonality shaping.

## **Acoustic Defect Detection Methodologies**

In the absence of calibrated magnitude data, the system must leverage the relationships between different frequency bands, the timing of the impulse response, and the spatial variance between individual speaker sweeps. A functional speaker operating in a standard automotive door will exhibit predictable acoustic behavior. By analyzing deviations from these predictions, the system can identify specific hardware or installation failures.  
Mechanical defects, such as a damaged speaker cone, a loose mounting baffle, or a poorly secured door panel, introduce non-linearities into the system. A rattling door panel, for example, acts as a secondary acoustic radiator. Because the metal or plastic panel possesses low internal damping, it will ring continuously when excited by its resonant frequency. In the frequency domain, this out-of-phase radiation often cancels the primary sound from the speaker, resulting in a severe, localized null in the ![][image13]\-octave measurement1. In the time domain, the high-Q mechanical resonance manifests as a prolonged decay tail in the impulse response14. By cross-referencing the frequency of the null with the decay characteristics of the impulse response, the algorithm can reliably diagnose a mounting failure.  
Electrical defects, particularly polarity inversions in passive two-way component sets, present a different algorithmic signature. When a tweeter is wired in reverse polarity relative to its mid-woofer, the acoustic summation at the passive crossover frequency becomes highly destructive. This creates a deep, wide cancellation notch in the frequency response16. While boundary reflections (comb filtering) can also create deep notches, a polarity inversion alters the primary arrival of the impulse response, whereas a physical reflection creates a distinct, secondary voltage spike delayed by the time it took the sound wave to travel the extra distance bouncing off a window12.  
The following sections address the specific acoustic parameters, dimensional averages, and detection thresholds required to build the diagnostic logic, strictly adhering to the requested format of a structured data table followed by a concise analytical paragraph.

The interior acoustic dimensions of a vehicle are significantly smaller than the exterior footprint, dictating the fundamental boundaries for modal frequencies and pneumatic pressurization. Length is measured from the lowest forward point of the front footwell to the rear acoustic boundary—which, in a sedan, extends through the acoustically transparent rear seats to the trunk bulkhead, and in hatchbacks or SUVs, extends to the tailgate glass7. Width is constrained by the inward curve of the B-pillars and side glass at shoulder height, while height spans from the floor pan to the headliner, heavily influenced by the presence of under-floor components or sunroof mechanisms5.

Cabin gain marks the transition of the vehicle interior from a resonant wave-guide to a sealed pneumatic chamber, occurring when half the acoustic wavelength exceeds the longest interior dimension2. Because low-frequency waves easily pass through standard automotive seat foam, a sedan's trunk volume directly couples to the cabin, pushing the effective acoustic length backward and lowering the onset frequency7. Hatchbacks and SUVs operate as a single contiguous volume, yielding similar behavior. In a perfectly sealed vehicle, the resulting pressure-zone gain boosts frequencies below the onset point at a theoretical rate of ![][image47], resulting in a massive natural enhancement of ![][image49] to ![][image50] in the lowest sub-bass registers3. Introducing leaks through open windows or sunroofs bleeds off this pneumatic pressure, halving the slope to roughly ![][image51], while lowering a cabriolet roof entirely eradicates the boundary conditions, leaving zero cabin gain and returning the system to half-space radiation4.

While the theoretical axial mode equation predicts distinct standing waves based on length, width, and height, a fully trimmed automotive cabin containing seats, carpets, and human occupants acts as a highly effective broadband absorber2. This severe boundary damping prevents sharp, distinct resonances; instead, cabin modes are heavily damped, exhibiting broad Q values of ![][image54] to ![][image55] and overlapping significantly to create wide humps or dips of ![][image54] to ![][image58]1. Above ![][image53], modal density becomes so high and damping so severe that individual axial modes cease to be discernible, blending into a diffuse field. To algorithmically distinguish a true cabin mode from a mechanical panel resonance using a fixed microphone, the system must cross-reference all speaker sweeps; a cabin mode is a property of the global volume and will appear at the exact same frequency regardless of which speaker excites the room, whereas a door resonance is localized and only appears when that specific door's speaker is driven1.

When a speaker adapter ring is cracked or improperly sealed to the inner door skin, it typically vibrates at lower frequencies, creating mechanical rattling around ![][image65]14. Conversely, loose plastic interior door cards or poorly damped outer metal skins tend to resonate sympathetically at higher mid-bass frequencies, commonly near ![][image66]14. Because these materials lack significant internal acoustic damping, their mechanical Q factor is quite high, meaning they ring persistently when excited15. In a single-point ![][image13]\-octave measurement, this out-of-phase mechanical vibration actively cancels the direct acoustic wave from the speaker cone, manifesting as a sharp cancellation dip of ![][image63] to ![][image64]1. In the time domain, the impulse response will show an abnormally long, high-frequency decay tail isolated strictly to the sweep of the defective channel.

### **5\. Tweeter-Versus-Woofer Polarity Inversion in a Two-Way Component Set**

| Quantity | Value or Range | Mark | Source |

| Reflection Delay (Comb Filter) | ![][image70] to ![][image71] | Theoretical | 12 |
| Comb Filter Path Difference | ![][image49] to ![][image72] | Rule of thumb | 16 |

Passive two-way component networks in automotive applications typically divide the audio spectrum between ![][image73] and ![][image68]32. If the tweeter is wired with inverted polarity, the destructive interference at the crossover point creates a massive energy void, visible in the ![][image13]\-octave bands as a severe ![][image63] to ![][image69] dip1. Because a fixed microphone cannot be moved to verify if the dip shifts in frequency (the standard test for a spatial comb filter), the system must rely on the impulse response. A comb-filter notch caused by a windshield reflection results from the sound traveling an extra ![][image49] to ![][image72], which produces a distinct, secondary voltage spike in the impulse response arriving ![][image70] to ![][image71] after the initial direct sound12. An electrical polarity inversion, however, creates no such delayed reflection; instead, the primary attack of the impulse response will plunge deep into the negative domain before rebounding, revealing the tweeter's reversed absolute phase17.

In a left-hand drive vehicle, the driver's seat (or fascia microphone) suffers extreme acoustic asymmetry. The left door speaker is vastly closer to the sensor than the right door speaker, generating an inherent Time of Arrival delay difference of ![][image84] to ![][image85]12. Below ![][image86], where sound is omnidirectional, the left channel will naturally record ![][image77] to ![][image78] louder strictly due to the inverse square law of distance propagation12. In the midrange and treble, directivity beaming causes the difference to narrow slightly, but the left channel typically remains ![][image80] to ![][image81] louder12. The diagnostic algorithm considers these predictable geometric imbalances as the baseline. A hardware defect—such as a blown tweeter, an obstructed mid-woofer, or catastrophic wiring failure—is only flagged when the amplitude disparity between the left and right pair exceeds ![][image64] in a specific ![][image13]\-octave band12.

### **7\. Front Versus Rear**

| Quantity | Value or Range | Mark | Source |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Broadband Level Difference | Rear is ![][image54] to ![][image58] lower | Rule of thumb | 35 |
| High-Frequency Attenuation (![][image87]) | Additional ![][image77] to ![][image78] drop | Rule of thumb | 35 |
| Time Delay Difference | Rear arrives ![][image88] later | Measured | 35 |

Measurements taken from the front fascia heavily bias toward the front door speakers, rendering the rear doors and parcel shelf speakers at a severe acoustic disadvantage. The physical bulk of the driver and passenger seats acts as a massive broadband acoustic barricade, heavily absorbing mid and high frequencies before they reach the dashboard35. As a result, it is completely normal for rear channels to measure ![][image54] to ![][image58] quieter than the front channels across the entire spectrum35. Furthermore, wavelengths shorter than the seat dimensions (above ![][image89]) suffer extreme attenuation, often resulting in an additional ![][image77] to ![][image78] roll-off in the upper treble bands35. The auto-EQ system must recognize this steep high-frequency deficit as a natural consequence of interior vehicle geometry, not as a pair of blown rear tweeters.

The Harman in-car target curve defines the psychoacoustically optimal steady-state room response for an enclosed vehicle, explicitly incorporating the natural physics of cabin gain into its design1. A mathematically flat response inside a car sounds thin and fatiguing due to the masking effects of low-frequency road noise and human equal-loudness contours (ISO 226\)36. Therefore, the target demands a bass shelf peaking around ![][image95] near ![][image113] to ![][image66], maintaining slight warmth through the mid-bass, achieving a slight vocal presence lift around ![][image114], and executing a smooth, continuous roll-off to ![][image112] at the highest frequencies3. If the measurement environment is designated as an open space (e.g., a test bench or a convertible with the roof down), the system must dynamically flatten the target curve below ![][image115]. In the absence of boundary structures, attempting to force a ![][image116] cabin-gain bass shelf using global EQ will instantly overdrive the amplifiers and destroy the woofers, as the physical mechanism for pressure-zone gain no longer exists27.

## **Advanced System Diagnostics and Algorithmic Logic**

To process the acoustic inputs effectively given the limitations of the ROHM BU32107 DSP, the head unit relies heavily on boolean logic derived from cross-referencing multi-channel sweeps. The global EQ topology prevents the correction of individual channel anomalies, forcing the software to act primarily as an automated diagnostic tool.  
When the raw ![][image13]\-octave band values and the GCC-PHAT time-delay vectors are extracted, the microcontroller processes the data through a decision tree. First, it verifies geometric sanity: in a left-hand drive vehicle, the left door's initial impulse response must arrive sooner than the right door's. If the algorithm detects that the right channel arrives first or is broadband louder than the left channel at the fascia microphone, it immediately flags a severe wiring harness error or a blocked microphone pinhole.  
Second, the system isolates mechanical resonances. Because the ![][image4]\-band EQ operates at a fixed Q of ![][image9] (yielding a ![][image12]\-octave bandwidth)13, attempting to flatten a narrow door-panel rattle will indiscriminately pull down adjacent, healthy frequencies, destroying the tonality of the system1. Therefore, when a sharp dip is detected in the ![][image66] band on only one channel, accompanied by extended time-domain ringing, the system refuses to apply EQ. Instead, it generates a plain-language user alert identifying the specific door requiring physical sound-deadening material. Only broadband deviations that span multiple ![][image13]\-octave bands across *all* speakers are eligible for the global ![][image117] EQ correction, allowing the system to gently tilt the overall cabin response toward the Harman target without chasing localized phase cancellations.

| **Extreme Distance Asymmetry (Mic Blocked or Harness Reversed)** | GCC-PHAT arrival time for Left channel is delayed relative to Right channel, or overall broadband level of Left is quieter than Right. | It is geometrically impossible in a LHD car for the left door to be further or quieter than the right door at the dashboard fascia. | **Absolute.** Warn owner: "Microphone is obstructed, or Left/Right speaker outputs are wired backwards at the harness." |
